title: Of cruelty
paragraphs: I take virtue to be something other, and something nobler, than good nature and the mere leaning toward goodness we are born into the world with. Well-disposed and well-descended souls do indeed follow the same paths, and present in their actions the same face that virtue itself does; but the word virtue carries with it, I don't quite know what, more great and active than just letting oneself be gently and quietly drawn, by a happy disposition, into the rule of reason. The man who, by a natural sweetness and easiness of nature, would shrug off injuries received, would no doubt do a very fine and praiseworthy thing; but the man who, provoked and stung to the quick by some offence, fortifies himself with the arms of reason against the furious appetite for revenge, and, after a great struggle, masters his own passion, certainly does a great deal more. The first does well; the second virtuously. One action might be called goodness, the other virtue; for, to my mind, the very name of virtue presupposes difficulty and contention, and cannot be exercised without an opponent. It is for this reason, perhaps, that we call God good, mighty, generous, and just, but we do not call Him virtuous, since all His operations are natural and without effort. It has been the opinion of many philosophers, not only Stoics but Epicureans — and this addition —

[Montaigne stops here to make his excuse for naming the Epicureans alongside the Stoics, in conformity with the common opinion that the Epicureans were not so rigid in their morals as the Stoics — which is not true in the main, as he demonstrates at a stroke. This involved Montaigne in a tedious parenthesis, during which the reader had best stay attentive, so as not to lose the thread of the argument entirely. In some later editions of this author it has been tried to remedy this inconvenience, but without noticing that Montaigne's argument is made weaker and more obscure by such vain repetitions: it is a licence that ought not to be taken, because whoever publishes another man's work ought to give it as the other composed it. In Mr Cotton's translation, however, he was so puzzled by this enormous parenthesis that he left it out altogether. — Coste.]

I am borrowing here from the common opinion, which is false — for all the witty remark of Arcesilaus in answer to someone who, reproached that many students went from his school to that of Epicurus but never any from Epicurus to him, replied, "I quite believe it; plenty of capons are made out of cocks, but never any cocks out of capons." For, in truth, the Epicurean sect is in no way inferior to the Stoic in steadiness and in the rigour of its opinions and precepts. And a certain Stoic, showing more honesty than those disputants who, in order to pick a quarrel with Epicurus and throw the game into their own hands, made him say things he never thought — putting a wrong construction on his words, dressing his sentences, by strict grammar, in another meaning and a different opinion from what they knew he held in his mind and in his morals — that Stoic, I say, declared that he abandoned the Epicurean sect among other reasons because he found their road too lofty and inaccessible;
["And those are called lovers of pleasure, who are in effect lovers of honour and justice, and who cultivate and observe all the virtues." — Cicero, Ep. Fam., xv. 1, 19.]

These philosophers say that it is not enough to have the soul seated in a good place, of a good temper, and well disposed toward virtue; it is not enough to have our resolutions and our reasoning fixed above all the power of fortune; we must also seek out occasions to put them to the proof. They would seek pain, hardship, and contempt to contend with, to keep the soul in breath:
"Multum sibi adjicit virtus lacessita."
["Virtue when assailed adds much to its own strength." — Seneca, Ep., 13.]

This is one of the reasons why Epaminondas, who belonged to yet a third sect, refused the riches fortune offered him by very lawful means — because, he said, he had to contend with poverty; in which extreme he kept himself to the last. Socrates put himself, I think, to a still harder test, keeping for his exercise a confounded scolding wife — a sparring partner with sharp blades. Metellus, alone of all the Roman senators, having attempted, by the power of virtue, to withstand the violence of Saturninus, tribune of the people at Rome, who was bent on passing an unjust law in favour of the commons — and, by so doing, having incurred the capital penalties Saturninus had set against the dissenters — addressed those who, in this extremity, were leading him to execution with words to this effect: that it was too easy and too base to do ill; and that to do well where there was no danger was a common thing; but that to do well where there was danger was the proper office of a man of virtue. Metellus's words show very clearly what I want to make out: that virtue refuses ease for a companion; that the easy, smooth, downhill way along which the regular steps of a sweet disposition are conducted is not the way of true virtue; she demands a rough and stormy passage. She wants either outward difficulties to wrestle with — like Metellus's, by means of which fortune delights to interrupt the speed of her career — or inward difficulties, brought on by the disordered appetites and imperfections of our condition to disturb her.

I have come this far at my ease; but here it comes into my head that, by this rule, the soul of Socrates — the most perfect that ever came to my knowledge — would deserve very little recommendation; for I cannot conceive in that person any movement at all of vicious inclination. I cannot imagine there could have been any difficulty or constraint in the course of his virtue. I know his reason to be so powerful and sovereign over him that she would never have allowed a vicious appetite so much as to stir in him. To a virtue so elevated as his, I have nothing to oppose. I think I see him march with a victorious and triumphant step, in pomp and at his ease, without opposition or trouble. If virtue can only shine bright by the conflict of contrary appetites, are we to say she cannot subsist without the assistance of vice, and that it is to vice she owes her reputation and honour? What then would become of that brave and generous Epicurean pleasure that prides itself on cherishing virtue tenderly in its lap, and letting it play and frolic there, giving it for toys shame, fevers, poverty, death, and torments? If I suppose that a perfect virtue shows itself in contending, in patiently enduring pain, and bearing the utmost extremity of the gout without being moved from her seat; if I give her troubles and difficulty for her necessary objects — what will become of a virtue elevated to such a degree as not only to despise pain but to rejoice in it, and be tickled by the throes of a sharp colic, such as the Epicureans set up, and of which many of them, in their actions, have given the clearest proof? As have several others, who I find to have surpassed in deed even the very rules of their discipline. Witness the younger Cato: when I see him die, tearing out his own bowels, I am not satisfied to believe simply that his soul was at that moment wholly free from trouble and horror; I cannot think he merely kept himself in the steadiness the Stoic rules prescribed for him — temperate, without emotion, undisturbed. There was, I think, something in this man's virtue too lively and fresh to stop there. I believe that, without doubt, he felt a pleasure and a delight in so noble an action, and was more pleased in it than in any other of his life:
"Sic abiit a vita, ut causam moriendi nactum se esse gauderet."
["He so departed from life, rejoicing that a reason for dying had been given him." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 30.]

I believe it so thoroughly that I question whether he would have been content to be deprived of the occasion of so brave an exploit; and if the goodness that made him embrace the public cause more than his own did not hold me back, I should easily fall into the opinion that he held himself obliged to fortune for having put his virtue to so brave a trial, and for having favoured that thief in trampling underfoot the ancient liberty of his country. I think I read in this action I know not what exaltation in his soul, and an extraordinary, manly stirring of pleasure, when he looked on the generosity and height of his enterprise:
"Deliberata morte ferocior,"
["The more fierce for having resolved on death." — Horace, Od., i. 37, 29.]

not goaded by any hope of glory, as the vulgar and effeminate judgments of some have concluded (for that consideration was too mean and low to take hold of so generous, so haughty, and so determined a heart as his), but for the very beauty of the thing in itself, which he, who had the handling of the springs, saw more clearly and in its full perfection than we are able to. Philosophy has obliged me by deciding that so brave an action would have been out of place in any other life than Cato's, and that it belonged only to his to end so. Nevertheless, and according to reason, he commanded his son and the senators who accompanied him to take another course in their affairs:

"Catoni, quum incredibilem natura tribuisset gravitatem, eamque ipse perpetua constantia roboravisset, semperque in proposito consilio permansisset, moriendum potius, quam tyranni vultus aspiciendus, erat."

["Cato, whom nature had endowed with an incredible gravity, which he had fortified by perpetual constancy, ever remaining of his predetermined resolve, had rather to die than to look on the face of a tyrant." — Cicero, De Off., i. 31.]

Every death ought to hold proportion with the life that went before it; we do not become other people for dying. I always interpret the death by the preceding life; and if anyone tells me of a death strong and steady in appearance attached to a feeble life, I conclude it was produced by some feeble cause and was of a piece with the life before. Then is not the easiness of his death, and the facility of dying that he had acquired by the vigour of his soul, something to be reckoned to him? Are we to say it should take anything from the lustre of his virtue? And who, with the least tincture of true philosophy in his brain, can be content to imagine Socrates only as free from fear and passion in the affair of his prison, his fetters, and his condemnation — and not discover in him not just firmness and constancy (which was his ordinary state), but, on top of that, I do not know what new satisfaction, a frolic cheerfulness in his last words and actions? In the start he gave at the pleasure of scratching his leg when his irons were taken off, does he not show an equal serenity and joy in his soul at being freed from past inconveniences, and at the same time entering into the knowledge of things to come? Cato will pardon me, please; his death is indeed more tragic and more lingering, but this one, somehow, is the finer. To one who lamented this death, Aristippus said: "May the gods grant me such a one." In the souls of these two great men, and of their imitators (for I much doubt whether they ever had their equals), one sees so perfect a habit of virtue that it had turned into a temperament. It is no longer a laborious virtue, nor the precepts of reason, to maintain which the soul has to be racked; it is the very essence of their soul, its natural and ordinary disposition. They have made it so by a long practice of philosophical precepts, having lit upon a rich and fine nature; the vicious passions that spring up in us can find no entrance into them; the force and vigour of their soul stifle and extinguish disordered desires the moment they begin to stir.

Now, that it is nobler — by a high and divine resolution — to prevent the very birth of temptations, and to be so formed to virtue that the very seeds of vice are rooted out, than to check by main force their growth and, having let oneself be caught by the first stirrings of the passions, to arm oneself and stand firm against their progress and overcome them; and that this second effect is more generous still than simply being endowed with an easy, affable nature, by itself averse to debauchery and vice — I do not think can be doubted. For this third and last sort of virtue seems to make a man innocent, but not virtuous; free from doing ill, but not very apt to do well. Considering also that this condition is so close a neighbour to imperfection and cowardice that I hardly know how to draw the boundary line between them. The very names of goodness and innocence have, for this reason, fallen into a certain contempt. I know well enough that several virtues — chastity, sobriety, temperance — may come to a man through personal defects. Constancy in danger, if it must be so called, the contempt of death, and patience in misfortunes can often be found in men through lack of judging such accidents rightly, through not grasping them for what they are. Want of comprehension and stupidity sometimes counterfeit virtuous effects, as I have often seen happen: men have been commended for what really deserved blame. An Italian lord once said this in my presence, to the disadvantage of his own nation: that the subtlety of the Italians and the vivacity of their conceptions were so great, and they foresaw the dangers and accidents that might befall them so far ahead, that it was not strange they were often, in war, observed providing for their safety even before they had seen the peril; that we French and the Spaniards, who were not so cunning, would go further, and had to be made to see and feel the danger before we would take the alarm — but even then we could not stick to it; while the Germans and Swiss, more gross and heavy, did not have the sense to look about them even when the blows were falling about their ears. He perhaps spoke this way only for mirth's sake; and yet it is most certain that in war, raw soldiers rush into dangers more recklessly than after they have been beaten about a bit*. (The original has eschauldex — scalded.)
"Haud ignarus . . . quantum nova gloria in armis, Et praedulce decus, primo certamine possit."
["Not unaware how much the fresh glory of arms and the sweetest honour can do in the first contest." — Aeneid, xi. 154.]
It is for this reason that, when we judge of a particular action, we have to consider the circumstances and the whole man by whom it was performed before we give it a name.

To take myself as an example: I have sometimes known my friends call that prudence in me which was sheer chance, and put down to courage and patience what was really judgment and opinion, attributing one title to me instead of another, sometimes to my advantage and sometimes the other way. For the rest, I am so far from having arrived at the first and most perfect degree of excellence, in which virtue is turned into a habit, that even of the second I have given no great proof. I have not been very busy to bridle the desires that have plagued me. My virtue is a virtue — or rather an innocence — of chance and accident. If I had been born with a more disordered temperament, I am afraid I should have made a sorry showing; for I have never noticed any great stability in my soul to resist passions, however slight their force. I do not know how to nurse quarrels and debates within my own bosom, and consequently owe myself no great thanks for being free from a number of vices:
"Si vitiis mediocribus et mea paucis Mendosa est natura, alioqui recta, velut si Egregio inspersos reprehendas corpore naevos:"
["If my nature is marred by only slight and few vices, and is otherwise sound, it is as if you should reproach moles on a fine body." — Horace, Sat., i. 6, 65.]

I owe it rather to my fortune than to my reason. She has caused me to be descended from a race famous for integrity, and from a very good father; I do not know whether he passed some of his temper on to me, or whether domestic example and the good upbringing of my infancy insensibly helped the work, or whether I was simply born that way:
"Seu Libra, seu me Scorpius adspicit Formidolosus, pars violentior Natalis horae, seu tyrannus Hesperiae Capricornus undae:"
["Whether the Balance, or dread Scorpio (the more violent over my natal hour), or Capricorn, tyrant of the Hesperian sea, looks down on me." — Horace, Od., ii. 17.]

but so it is, that I have a natural horror for most vices. The answer of Antisthenes to one who asked him what was the best apprenticeship — "to unlearn evil" — seems to point at this. I hold them in horror, I say, with a loathing so natural, and so much my own, that the same instinct and impression I brought with me from my nurse, I still retain, and no temptation whatever has had the power to make me change it. Not even my own discourses, which on certain things break out of the common track and might seem easily to license me for actions my natural inclination makes me hate. I will say a strange thing, but I will say it: I find myself, in many ways, more under restraint by my manners than by my opinions, and my desires less debauched than my reason. Aristippus put forward such bold opinions in favour of pleasure and riches that he set all the philosophers against him; but as for his manners — Dionysius the tyrant, having presented three beautiful women for him to choose from, he answered that he would have all three, and that Paris had got himself into trouble for preferring one over the other two — but having taken them home, he sent them back untouched. His servant, finding himself overburdened on the road with the money he was carrying after him, Aristippus ordered him to pour out and throw away as much as troubled him. And Epicurus, whose doctrines were so irreligious and effeminate, was in his life very laborious and devout; he wrote to a friend that he lived only on biscuit and water, begging him to send him a little cheese to keep by him for when he had a mind to make a feast. Must it be true that to be a perfectly good man one must be so by some hidden, natural, and universal property, without law, reason, or example? The debauches in which I have been engaged have not, thank God, been of the worst sort, and I have condemned them in myself — for my judgment was never infected by them; on the contrary, I accuse them more severely in myself than in anyone else. But that is all, for, as to the rest, I put up too little resistance and let myself lean too much to the other side of the scale, except that I moderate them, and prevent them from mixing with other vices, which for the most part will cling together if one is not careful. I have shortened and curtailed mine, to make them as single and as simple as I can:
"Nec ultra Errorem foveo."
["Nor do I push my error further." — Juvenal, viii. 164.]

As for the opinion of the Stoics, who say, "That the wise man, when he acts, acts by all the virtues together, though one is most apparent according to the nature of the action" (and here the analogy of a human body might serve them somewhat, for the action of anger cannot work unless all the humours assist it, though choler predominates) — if they want to draw a like consequence, that when the wicked man does wickedly he does it by all the vices together, I do not believe it, or else I do not understand them, for I find by experience the contrary. These are sharp, unsubstantial subtleties with which philosophy sometimes amuses itself. I follow some vices, but I flee others as much as a saint would. The Peripatetics also reject this indissoluble connection; and Aristotle is of opinion that a prudent and just man may be intemperate and inconstant. Socrates confessed to some who had detected a certain inclination to vice in his physiognomy that it was, in truth, his natural leaning, but that he had corrected it by discipline. And those who were familiar with the philosopher Stilpo said that, being born with an addiction to wine and women, he had by study rendered himself very abstinent from both.

What I have in me of good, I have, on the contrary, by the chance of my birth; and I hold it not by law, precept, or any other instruction. The innocence that is in me is a simple thing — little vigour and no art. Among other vices, I mortally hate cruelty, both by nature and by judgment, as the very extreme of all vices: so much so that I cannot see a chicken's neck pulled off without distress, and cannot endure without impatience the cry of a hare in my dog's teeth, though the chase is a violent pleasure of mine. Those who have to fight with sensuality readily make use of this argument to show that it is wholly vicious and unreasonable — that when it is at its height it overpowers us to such a degree that reason can have no access — and they cite our own experience in the act of love,
"Quum jam praesagit gaudia corpus, Atque in eo est Venus, ut muliebria conserat arva."

where they hold that pleasure so transports us that our reason cannot do its office while we are in such ecstasy and rapture. I know very well it can be otherwise, and that a man may sometimes, if he wishes, gain this point over himself — to bend his soul, even at the critical moment, to think of something else; but he has to bend it to that hard. I know one may triumph over the utmost effort of this pleasure: I have tried it on myself, and have not found Venus so imperious a goddess as many, much more virtuous men than I, declare. I do not consider it a miracle, as the Queen of Navarre does in one of the Tales of her Heptameron (which is a very pretty book of its kind), nor a thing of extreme difficulty, to pass whole nights, with all the convenience and liberty one could wish, with a long-coveted mistress, and yet keep the pledge first given to satisfy oneself with kisses and similar caresses, without pressing any further. The example of the pleasure of the chase, I think, would be more apt: where, though the pleasure is less, there is the higher excitement of unexpected joy, leaving no time for reason, taken by surprise, to prepare itself for the encounter — when, after a long quest, the beast suddenly starts up in a place where one perhaps least expected it; the shock and ardour of the shouts and cries of the hunters strike us so that it would be hard for those who love this lesser chase to turn their thoughts, at that instant, another way. The poets make Diana triumph over the torch and arrows of Cupid:
"Quis non malarum, quas amor curas habet, Haec inter obliviscitur?"
["Who, amid such delights, would not forget the anxious cares of love?" — Horace, Epod., ii. 37.]

To return to what I was saying: I am tenderly moved by the afflictions of others, and would readily cry for company, if, on any occasion at all, I could cry. Nothing draws tears from me except tears — and not only real and true ones, but whatever they are, feigned or painted. I do not much mourn the dead, and would envy them rather; but I greatly mourn the dying. The savages do not offend me so much by roasting and eating the bodies of the dead as those do who torment and persecute the living. Indeed, I cannot watch even the ordinary executions of justice, however reasonable, with a steady eye. Someone, to give evidence of Julius Caesar's clemency, says: "He was mild in his revenges. Having forced the pirates to surrender — those by whom he had earlier been taken prisoner and put to ransom — and forasmuch as he had threatened them with the cross, he did indeed condemn them to it, but only after they had been first strangled. He punished his secretary Philemon, who had attempted to poison him, with no greater severity than mere death." Without naming this Latin author, who dares to allege as a testimony of mercy the killing only of those by whom we have been offended, it is easy to guess that he was shocked by the horrid and inhuman examples of cruelty practised by the Roman tyrants.

For my part, even in justice itself, all that exceeds a simple death seems to me sheer cruelty — especially in us, who, having a regard for souls, ought to dismiss them in a good and calm condition; which cannot be when we have agitated them with insufferable torments. Not long ago a soldier, who was a prisoner, perceiving from a tower where he was shut up that people were beginning to gather at the place of execution and that the carpenters were busy putting up a scaffold, concluded straight away that the preparation was for him and made up his mind to kill himself. He could find no instrument to help him in his design except an old rusty cart-nail that fortune put in his hand; with this he first gave himself two great wounds about his throat, but finding these would not do, he gave himself a third in the belly, where he left the nail sticking up to the head. The first of his keepers who came in found him in this condition — still alive, but sunk down and exhausted by his wounds. So as to make use of the time before he died, they hurried to read his sentence; and when he heard that he was only condemned to be beheaded, he seemed to take new courage, accepted wine he had earlier refused, and thanked his judges for the unhoped-for mildness of their sentence; saying that he had decided to dispatch himself for fear of a more severe and unbearable death, having taken it, from the preparations he had seen on the spot, that they meant to torment him with some horrible execution; and that he felt delivered from death in having it changed from what he had feared.

I would advise that those examples of severity, by which it is meant to keep the people in their duty, should be exercised upon the dead bodies of criminals. To see them deprived of burial, to see them boiled and divided into quarters, would work nearly as much upon the crowd as the pain inflicted on the living — although in effect this last is little or nothing, as God himself says: "Who kill the body, and after that have no more that they can do." And the poets dwell especially on the horrors of this picture as something worse than death:
"Heu! reliquias semiustas regis, denudatis ossibus, Per terram sanie delibutas foede divexarier."
["Alas! that the half-burnt remains of the king, with the bones exposed, should be foully dragged along the ground, smeared with gore." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., i. 44.]

I happened to come by, one day at Rome, just as they were executing Catena, a notorious robber. He was strangled without any emotion in the spectators; but when they came to cut him in quarters, the hangman gave no blow that the people did not follow with a doleful cry and exclamation, as if each one had lent his sense of feeling to the wretched carcass. Those inhuman excesses should be exercised on the bark, not on the living wood. Artaxerxes, in nearly the same case, moderated the severity of the ancient laws of Persia, ordaining that the nobility who had committed a fault, instead of being whipped as they used to be, should be stripped only and have their clothes whipped for them; and that, whereas they used to have their hair torn out, they should only have their high-crowned tiara taken off. The very devout Egyptians thought they sufficiently satisfied divine justice by sacrificing hogs in effigy and representation — a bold invention, to pay God so essential a substance in mere picture and show.

I live in a time when we abound in incredible examples of this vice, through the licence of our civil wars; and we see nothing in ancient histories more extreme than what we have proof of every day. But I cannot, for all that, get used to it. I could hardly persuade myself, before I saw it with my own eyes, that there could be found souls so cruel and savage that, for the sole pleasure of murder, would commit it — would hack and lop off the limbs of others, sharpen their wits to invent unusual torments and new kinds of death, without hatred, without profit, for no other end than to enjoy the pleasing spectacle of the gestures and motions, the lamentable groans and cries of a man dying in anguish. For this is the utmost point to which cruelty can come:
"Ut homo hominem, non iratus, non timens, tantum spectaturus, occidat."
["That a man should kill a man, not being angry, not being in fear, only for the sake of the spectacle." — Seneca, Ep., 90.]

For my own part, I cannot, without grief, see so much as an innocent beast pursued and killed which has no defence and has done us no offence at all; and what often happens — that the stag we are hunting, finding himself weak and out of breath, and seeing no other remedy, surrenders himself to us his pursuers, imploring mercy by his tears —
"Questuque cruentus, Atque imploranti similis,"
["Who, bleeding, by his moans seems to beg for mercy." — Aeneid, vii. 501.]
has always been to me a very unpleasing sight; and I hardly ever take a beast alive that I do not at once turn out again. Pythagoras bought them from fishermen and fowlers to do the same:
"Primoque a caede ferarum, Incaluisse puto maculatum sanguine ferrum."
["I think it was the slaughter of wild beasts that first warmed up the steel of man, stained with blood." — Ovid, Met., xv. 106.]

Those natures that are bloodthirsty toward beasts show a natural proneness to cruelty. After the Romans had grown accustomed to spectacles of the slaughter of animals, they went on to those of the slaughter of men, of gladiators. Nature herself has, I fear, imprinted in man a kind of instinct toward inhumanity; nobody takes pleasure in seeing beasts play and caress one another, but everyone delights in seeing them tear and dismember each other. And so that I may not be laughed at for the sympathy I feel for them — theology itself enjoins us some favour on their behalf; and considering that one and the same master has lodged us together in this palace for his service, and that they, as well as we, are of his household, it has reason to enjoin upon us some affection and regard for them. Pythagoras borrowed the metempsychosis from the Egyptians, but it has since been received by several nations, and particularly by our Druids:
"Morte carent animae; semperque, priore relicta Sede, novis domibus vivunt, habitantque receptae."
["Souls do not die, but, having left their former seat, live in new dwellings, and are received and reside there." — Ovid, Met., xv. 158.]

The religion of our ancient Gauls held that souls, being eternal, never ceased to move from one body to another; and they mingled with this fancy some consideration of divine justice. For according to the deportments of the soul while it had been in Alexander, they said, God assigned it another body to inhabit, more or less painful, and suitable to its condition:
"Muta ferarum Cogit vincla pati; truculentos ingerit ursis, Praedonesque lupis; fallaces vulpibus addit: Atque ubi per varios annos, per mille figuras
Egit, Lethaeo purgatos flumine, tandem Rursus ad humanae revocat primordia formae:"

["He makes them bear the silent chains of brutes — the bloodthirsty souls he encloses in bears, the thieves in wolves, the deceivers in foxes; and when, through successive years and a thousand shapes, man has run his life, after their purging in Lethe's river, at last he calls them back to the original forms of human shape." — Claudian, In Ruf., ii. 482.]

If it had been brave, he lodged it in the body of a lion; if voluptuous, in a hog; if timorous, in a hart or a hare; if malicious, in a fox, and so for the rest, until — having purified it by this chastisement — it again entered the body of some other man:
"Ipse ego nam memini, Trojani tempore belli Panthoides Euphorbus eram."
["For I myself remember that, in the days of the Trojan war, I was Euphorbus, son of Panthus." — Ovid, Met., xv. 160; and see Diogenes Laertius, Life of Pythagoras.]

As to the kinship between us and the beasts, I do not much admit of it; nor of what several nations — and those among the most ancient and noble — have practised: who have not only taken brutes into their society and companionship, but have given them a rank infinitely above themselves, regarding them at one time as familiars and favourites of the gods, holding them in more than human reverence and respect; while others acknowledged no other god or divinity than they:
"Belluae a barbaris propter beneficium consecratae."
["Beasts were consecrated by barbarians out of opinion of some benefit they had had from them." — Cicero, De Natura Deor., i. 36.]
"Crocodilon adorat Pars haec; illa pavet saturam serpentibus ibin: Effigies sacri hic nitet aurea cercopitheci; Hic piscem fluminis, illic Oppida tota canem venerantur."

["This place adores the crocodile; that one dreads the ibis, gorged with serpents; here shines the golden image of the sacred ape; here men venerate the fish of the river; there whole towns worship a dog." — Juvenal, xv. 2.]

And the very interpretation Plutarch gives of this error — which is very well conceived — is in their favour: he says that it was not the cat or the ox, for example, that the Egyptians worshipped, but that in those beasts they worshipped some image of the divine faculties: in this, patience and usefulness; in that, vivacity; or, as with our neighbours the Burgundians and all the Germans, impatience at being shut up — by which they represented liberty, which they loved and adored above all other godlike attributes; and so of the rest. But when, among more moderate opinions, I come across arguments that try to demonstrate the near resemblance between us and animals — how large a share they have in our greatest privileges, and with how much probability they are compared with us — truly, I abate a great deal of our presumption, and willingly resign that imaginary sovereignty attributed to us over other creatures.

But supposing all this were not true, there is still a certain respect — a general duty of humanity — not only toward beasts that have life and sense, but even toward trees and plants. We owe justice to men, and graciousness and benignity to other creatures that are capable of it; there is a certain commerce and mutual obligation between them and us. Nor will I be afraid to confess the tenderness of my nature to be so childish that I cannot easily refuse to play with my dog when he, at the most inconvenient moments, presses me to do so. The Turks have alms and hospitals for beasts. The Romans took public care for the feeding of the geese, by whose vigilance their Capitol had been saved. The Athenians made a decree that the mules and donkeys that had served at the building of the temple called Hecatompedon should be free and allowed to pasture wherever they chose, without hindrance. The Agrigentines had a regular custom of solemnly burying the beasts they had a fondness for — horses of some rare quality, dogs, and useful birds, and even those that had only been kept to amuse their children; and the magnificence which was ordinary with them in other things also showed in the sumptuousness and number of the monuments raised for this purpose, monuments that remained in their beauty for several ages after. The Egyptians buried wolves, bears, crocodiles, dogs, and cats in sacred places, embalmed their bodies, and put on mourning at their death. Cimon gave an honourable burial to the mares with which he had three times gained the prize of the course at the Olympic Games. The ancient Xanthippus had his dog buried on an eminence near the sea, which has ever since kept the name; and Plutarch says he had a scruple about selling for a small profit to the slaughterer an ox that had long been in his service.
